1.pericope_label: Now in the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king’s commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, in the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, (though it was turned to the contrary, that the Jews had rule over them that hated them;) The Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, to lay hand on such as sought their hurt: and no man could withstand them; for the fear of them fell upon all people. And all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants, and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews; because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them. For Mordecai was great in the king’s house, and his fame went out throughout all the provinces: for this man Mordecai waxed greater and greater. Thus the Jews smote all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter, and destruction, and did what they would unto those that hated them. And in Shushan the palace the Jews slew and destroyed five hundred men. And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha, And Poratha, and Adalia, and Aridatha,

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch open with the shape of the whole chapter, that the Jews fought on the day both edicts had named and were supported by the royal officials, that Susa alone was granted a second day, and that the two fights ending a day apart is why one part of the nation rests on the fourteenth and the other on the fifteenth; they keep to the idiom elsewhere, that no one stood before them because the fear of them had fallen upon all people, and that the Jews did according to their will, which is to say retaliated at their own discretion. Ellicott doubts that the Jews confined themselves to standing for their lives. They had the whole executive of the empire on their side, the second edict was treated as repealing the first, and a people so lately in fear and now in favour at court were probably resolved to use their opportunity while they had it; who could object, he asks, so long as they did nothing against the authorities, and the numbers later reported show what use they made of it. He also notes that the verb rendered helped is literally lifted up, and that the palace must mean the whole royal city, since even Xerxes would hardly have allowed bloodshed inside the precincts.

Gill identifies the five hundred as men of Haman's faction headed by his ten sons, who took the decree as their occasion of revenge, the Targum calling them princes of the house of Amalek; he reads the place as the city in which the palace stood rather than the palace itself, since the Jews can hardly have had so many enemies at court. On the officers he notes that they did more than permit, the word meaning that they extolled and lifted the Jews up, and that Mordecai was by now the chief minister of state.

Clarke finds it strange that in a city where the king's mind must have been well known five hundred could be found to rise against those he befriended, and reads the record as clearing the Jews, since it does not appear that they slew any person who did not rise up to destroy them. Wesley agrees, taking those killed for men who would have watched every opportunity against them, and noting that the enemies did take up arms but were easily conquered.

Henry frames the day as a fair trial of skill, since neither side was surprised, both had long notice, and neither could call the other rebels, both being supported by the royal authority. He reports the Chaldee paraphrase that none appeared against the Jews but Amalekites only, infatuated and hardened as Pharaoh was, and adds that Haman's fall had exasperated rather than convinced his party. He credits the victory to their acting in concert rather than family by family, and turns the tag that forces act most powerfully when combined against the Jews of his own day, numerous and rich in many places and yet despicable because too selfish to incorporate. He rests the defence of the slaughter on necessity, the law of self-preservation with the king's decree behind it, and gives three reasons for the untouched spoil: a contempt of worldly wealth in imitation of Abraham refusing the spoils of Sodom, proof that they sought preservation and not enrichment, and humanity, since they might have destroyed the women and little ones and instead left them what would keep them alive. He also has the custom of reading the ten names in one breath, because they are held to have died in one moment.

debates.question: Did the Jews keep within the letter of their commission?

positions.position: Probably not, since they had the executive on their side and were resolved to use an opportunity they might not have again
Yes, since it does not appear that anyone was slain who had not risen up to destroy them
Justified in any case by necessity, the law of self-preservation standing behind the king's decree

debates.question: Why did anyone attack at all, with the court plainly against them?

positions.position: Because only Amalekites appeared, infatuated and hardened as Pharaoh was against Israel
Because Haman's faction was headed by his ten sons and took the decree as its occasion of revenge
No explanation offered, only the strangeness that five hundred could be found to do it where the king's mind was known

Turns the Jews' success in combining against the Jews of his own day, numerous and rich in many places and yet despicable because too selfish to incorporate.

10.pericope_label: The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand. On that day the number of those that were slain in Shushan the palace was brought before the king. And the king said unto Esther the queen, The Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men in Shushan the palace, and the ten sons of Haman; what have they done in the rest of the king’s provinces? now what is thy petition? and it shall be granted thee: or what is thy request further? and it shall be done. Then said Esther, If it please the king, let it be granted to the Jews which are in Shushan to do to morrow also according unto this day’s decree, and let Haman’s ten sons be hanged upon the gallows. And the king commanded it so to be done: and the decree was given at Shushan; and they hanged Haman’s ten sons. For the Jews that were in Shushan gathered themselves together on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar, and slew three hundred men at Shushan; but on the prey they laid not their hand.

schools.summary: Ellicott confirms in a line that the spoil might lawfully have been taken, and then refuses to defend the second day. Before the first day's slaughter was over the Jews were plainly out of danger, the sympathies of the court were with them and the king's officers had taken their part, so that after five hundred killed in the capital alone they were masters of the situation; he does not hesitate to call the fresh action needless butchery, calls the hanging of men already dead a gratuitous outrage, and says that because Esther was a person God used for a great purpose we are not called upon to tone down the black spots in her history, allowing only that she is not to be judged by the Christian standard. Keil and Delitzsch supply the practice behind the hanging, the bodies nailed up for the greater disgrace after a custom the law of the hanged malefactor also assumes, and add a point of construction, that the decree given at Susa is the permission to fight on the morrow rather than the order for the hanging, since it is that permission which accounts for the Jews assembling again, while the hanging is related in a subordinate clause.

Gill will not settle how the tally reached the king, leaving it between an order of the king's, who wanted to know how many enemies the Jews had in the city and how many of his own subjects had fallen, and an officious report by others meaning to irritate him against the Jews. On the decree for the fourteenth he keeps to the plain sense, that the Jews were given leave to seek out and slay the rest of their enemies in Susa as they had on the thirteenth.

Clarke says the Jews stood for their lives and gave full proof that they sought their own safety and not their enemies' property, though the decree had expressly authorised the spoil; on the second day he argues from information rather than probability, that Esther had likely learned from Mordecai how many had escaped, and notes that three hundred more were found, eight hundred in all, and the city purged. The hanging of the ten sons he takes for an exposure meant as a terror to those who sought the Jews' destruction. Wesley gives the motive for leaving the spoil, that it was left to the enemies' children so that what was done should appear to come not from malice or covetousness but from necessity and the great law of self-preservation; he supposes the worst of the enemies had hidden for the one day, after which the commission would expire and they would return home confidently, and reads the hanging as being for greater infamy and the terror of any who should presume to abuse the king in the like manner.

debates.question: Was the second day of slaughter justified?

positions.position: No; the Jews were already masters of the situation, and the fresh action was needless butchery
Yes; the worst of the enemies had hidden for the one day and would have returned safely once the commission expired
Yes; Esther had learned from Mordecai how many had escaped, and three hundred more were in fact found

debates.question: What does hanging add to men who were already dead?

positions.position: A terror to those who sought the Jews' destruction
Greater infamy, and the terror of any who should presume to abuse the king in the like manner
The customary disgrace of the exposed body, Hebrew and Persian alike
Nothing but a gratuitous outrage on the dead

Read the decree given at Susa as the permission to fight on the morrow rather than the order for the hanging, on the evidence of the verb forms and of the Jews assembling again on the fourteenth.

16.pericope_label: But the other Jews that were in the king’s provinces gathered themselves together, and stood for their lives, and had rest from their enemies, and slew of their foes seventy and five thousand, but they laid not their hands on the prey, On the thirteenth day of the month Adar; and on the fourteenth day of the same rested they, and made it a day of feasting and gladness. But the Jews that were at Shushan assembled together on the thirteenth day thereof, and on the fourteenth thereof; and on the fifteenth day of the same they rested, and made it a day of feasting and gladness. Therefore the Jews of the villages, that dwelt in the unwalled towns, made the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, and a good day, and of sending portions one to another.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the Greek version gives fifteen thousand rather than seventy-five, and thinks the smaller number perhaps the likelier; he then quotes Bishop Wordsworth to set the episode in a wider frame, that the history shows the recklessness of human life which then prevailed among the sovereigns of the East even towards their own subjects, and displays what would have followed for civilisation had Ahasuerus won at Salamis. On the country towns he works from the words rather than the custom, the two terms used being virtually one, meaning places undefended by bulwarks, the same term standing elsewhere in contrast with fenced cities; and he adds that both the fourteenth and the fifteenth are now kept as the feast, the earlier day being the chief. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the arithmetic of the two dates, that Susa was still fighting on the thirteenth and fourteenth and did not rest until the fifteenth, while the rest finished on the thirteenth and kept the fourteenth; they take the word introducing the statement about the country towns as the narrator's way of presenting the custom as a result of what precedes, and remark that the written form of the word for the unwalled places looks like an Aramaic variant.

Gill supplies the rule the later synagogue drew from the difference, reporting it from Jarchi: every place walled from the days of Joshua reads the book on the fifteenth of Adar and is called a walled town even if its walls are now gone, while a place unwalled then reads on the fourteenth and is called a city even if it is walled now. Shushan is the exception that shows how the rule was framed, since it was not walled in Joshua's day and yet reads on the fifteenth, because in it a miracle was done.

Clarke states the Susa side flatly, that two days were spent in slaying their enemies and the third in rest, and is the fullest on what the day was for: the villagers joined their rest to the preceding day and made it a time of festivity and of sending portions, by which he understands that the rich sent portions of what was killed for the occasion to the poor, so that they too might keep the day, and that as the sorrow had been general so also might the joy be. He also records a textual observation that unsettles the section he has just expounded, that the ancient Itala version omits the whole of these nineteen verses, and puts the question directly whether they were originally in the book, leaving it as a query he does not answer.

outliers.claim: Prefers the Greek version's fifteen thousand to the received seventy-five thousand, and is alone in doubting the number the chapter gives.
Notes that the ancient Itala version omits the whole of these nineteen verses and asks outright whether they were originally part of the book, leaving the question unanswered.
Reports from Jarchi the rule that fixes each town's day by whether it was walled in the days of Joshua, with Shushan excepted because a miracle was done in it.

20.pericope_label: And Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters unto all the Jews that were in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, both nigh and far, To stablish this among them, that they should keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar, and the fifteenth day of the same, yearly, As the days wherein the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month which was turned unto them from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a good day: that they should make them days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the settling of the feast as a ratification rather than a command, since the people had already begun by keeping both days and agreed to make it annual in consequence of Mordecai's letters. Ellicott marks the one thing actually added, that the provinces had already made the fourteenth their day of gladness and that what Mordecai now enjoins is the keeping of the fifteenth as well.

Gill takes what Mordecai wrote for the transactions of those two days with their causes, together with the letter that follows, and notes that some conclude from this that he was the penman of the book; he allows that he might have been, but will not have it follow necessarily. On the institution itself he glosses the ground of the whole, that these were the days on which the Jews rested from enemies who had risen up against them.

Clarke supposes the part written by Mordecai ends about here and that what follows was added by Ezra or the men of the Great Synagogue, though he grants the words may refer only to the letters sent into the provinces; either way the rest of the chapter is recapitulation with the institution of the feast attached.

Henry turns the authorship question into a comparison that does not favour Mordecai. Nehemiah at every turn notices divine Providence and the good hand of his God upon him, while Mordecai never so much as mentions the name of God in the whole story; the difference he lays to the two places, Jerusalem where religion was in fashion and an air of it appeared in common conversation, and Shushan where policy reigned more than piety, each man writing according to the genius of his place. He commends the one style and means to imitate it, and takes the other's lesson too, that men may be truly devout without abounding in the shows of devotion. He observes that the days kept are the days of rest and not the day of battle, as the sabbath was appointed not on the day God finished his work but on the day he rested from it, and that the feast falls a month before the passover so that the first and last month of the year both keep the memory of a deliverance. He disputes the later fast on the thirteenth, since the fasting belonged to the day of distress. The three prescriptions he reads as ascending, a day of cheerfulness, a day of generosity in the portions sent between friends, and a day of charity in the gifts going to the poor rather than to rich neighbours; and he records what the feast became on the testimony of Jewish writers themselves, commonly celebrated with gluttony and drunkenness and excess of riot.

debates.question: Did Mordecai write the book of Esther?

positions.position: Possibly, but it does not follow from his having written these things
His part ends about here, the remainder being added by Ezra or the men of the Great Synagogue
Many doubt it precisely because the name of God is never mentioned, and take the book for an extract from the Persian journals

outliers.claim: Observes that the days kept are the days of rest and not the day of the battle, as the sabbath was appointed not on the day God finished his work but on the day he rested from it.

Records what the feast became on the testimony of Jewish writers themselves, the Talmud saying that a man should drink at Purim until he cannot tell the difference between cursing Haman and blessing Mordecai.

23.pericope_label: And the Jews undertook to do as they had begun, and as Mordecai had written unto them; Because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to consume them, and to destroy them; But when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows. Wherefore they called these days Purim after the name of Pur. Therefore for all the words of this letter, and of that which they had seen concerning this matter, and which had come unto them, The Jews ordained, and took upon them, and upon their seed, and upon all such as joined themselves unto them, so as it should not fail, that they would keep these two days according to their writing, and according to their appointed time every year; And that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, every family, every province, and every city; and that these days of Purim should not fail from among the Jews, nor the memorial of them perish from their seed.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch argue that the clause about coming before the king is impersonal and means when the matter came rather than when Esther came, since she is not named anywhere in the context. They distinguish the two clauses that follow, the first giving the reason for the name and the second opening a fresh sentence that explains how the observance became general, on two grounds, the written injunction of Mordecai and the people's own experience of the event; and they gloss the phrase about the days not failing as a periphrasis for inviolably, the participles about remembering and keeping still depending on the clause that makes the observance perpetual. Ellicott reaches the impersonal reading from the printed page, pointing out that the name stands in italics in the English version because it is not in the Hebrew, which says only and on her or its coming, and that making the pronoun mean Esther is harsh when she has not been mentioned for some time. He describes the observance as it stands, kept on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar with the preceding day as a fast, the whole book read through in the synagogue service, a custom he traces to the Christian era on the evidence of Josephus and the older Jewish records.

Gill is careful about the kind of obligation assumed: the Jews engaged to keep the two days not in a religious but in a civil way, not as parts of worship nor as additions to the law, but in commemoration of a civil benefit received; and he reports that the scruple was raised anyway in later times, eighty five elders, more than thirty of them prophets, having been distressed about the matter for fear it was an innovation. He quotes the canon that makes the obligation exhaustive, priests, Levites, Nethinims, Israelites, men, women, proselytes and servants made free all obliged to read the book, with little ones trained up to read it; and he takes from Aben Ezra the reason for naming every province and every city, that it is precaution rather than decoration, set down lest a man think himself unbound where there are no Jews.

Clarke measures the undertaking by its result, that Mordecai wrote to bind them, their successors and their proselytes to an annual feast, that they undertook it, and that it has been observed among them in all the places of their dispersion from that day to this without any interruption. Wesley explains why the proselytes are included, since they were obliged to submit to other Jewish laws and had enjoyed the benefit of this deliverance, without which the nation and its religion would have been in great measure extinct; he notes too that the name is a Persian word for the lot.

outliers.claim: Reports that the feast was scrupled as an innovation in later times, eighty five elders and more than thirty prophets among them having been distressed about the matter.
Measures the undertaking by its survival, the feast having been kept in every place of the dispersion from that day to the present without any interruption.
Traces the reading of the whole book in the synagogue service back at least to the Christian era, on the evidence of Josephus and the older Jewish records.

29.pericope_label: Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority, to confirm this second letter of Purim. And he sent the letters unto all the Jews, to the hundred twenty and seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, with words of peace and truth, To confirm these days of Purim in their times appointed, according as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had enjoined them, and as they had decreed for themselves and for their seed, the matters of the fastings and their cry. And the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch translate the phrase as writing with all strength, which is to say very forcibly, and read the purpose as giving the letter's contents the force of law; they take this to be the second letter with reference to the one Mordecai had already sent through the provinces. On the fasting they reason from the suffix, which relates to the days of Purim and can therefore only mean portions of time within them, so that the fasting was appointed inside the festival rather than beside it. Ellicott counts the letters differently, taking the first to be the one Esther obtained from the king, so that the second is Mordecai's own, here confirmed in a more authoritative way. He admits the words about the fastings and the cry come in awkwardly, and that because the Greek version passes them over some have doubted them; but all the Hebrew copies and the other ancient versions keep them, so he concludes that the Jews had instituted fasts beyond what Mordecai enjoined, and connects this with the fast now kept on the thirteenth of Adar. He notes besides that one Hebrew verb stands behind the three English words for confirming, enjoining and decreeing, and that its force is simply to fix or settle, and is dissatisfied with taking the book to be this book, since that is hardly a natural way for an author to refer to the work he is writing.

Gill observes that Mordecai had before only recommended the festival and that the queen now gave it her sanction and laid her obligation on the Jews, guessing that some had been backward or had neglected it; he reports a Jewish chronologer dating the letter to the following year, and the older Targum's account that what they wrote was the whole volume, set down so as to put the deliverance in the strongest light. On the sending he notes that it was Mordecai who sent, signed in the queen's name and his own.

Clarke notes that the two of them had the king's licence and that their own authority was great, and draws attention to who is absent from the transaction: there is no mention of the approbation of any high priest, nor of any authority beyond that of Mordecai and Esther, the king being unable to join in a business belonging to a religion that was not the religion of his country. On the book he reports the versions rather than choosing between them, the Vulgate giving the clause a strange turn by making it cover everything contained in the history called Esther, the Targum saying that the roll was transcribed in this book, the Syriac agreeing with the Hebrew and the Greek not differing much. Wesley says more plainly that the former letter recommended and this one enjoins, because it was now not Mordecai's act only but the act of all the Jews binding themselves and their posterity, and supplies the occasion the words about the cry look back to, the calamities decreed against the whole nation, for the removing of which the Jews in every place had fled to God with fasting and strong cries.

debates.question: Which letter is the first, that this one is called the second?

positions.position: The letter Mordecai had already sent through the provinces

debates.question: What is the book in which the decree was written?

outliers.claim: Notes who is absent from the transaction, there being no approbation of any high priest and no authority beyond Mordecai and Esther, since the king could not join in a business belonging to a religion not his country's.
Defends the clause about the fastings and the cry against the doubt raised by its absence from the Greek version, on the ground that every Hebrew copy and every other ancient version retains it.
